passages.original: His ita absolutis, nihil deinceps Maximus de Antichristo, aut de postremo Domini adventu disserit, sed Ambrosium imitatus ad aperiendum verborum illorum sensum descendit, quæ sunt de duobus in lecto uno, deque duabus molentibus; atque hic inquit resurrectionis meritum demonstratur, quod pro qualitate vivendi sit gratia resurgendi: ac tantum in singulis quibusque resurrectionis esse distantiam, ut duobus pariter dormientibus, et una sede quiescentibus æqualis non possit esse assumptio.
passages.english: These matters having been thus concluded, Maximus says nothing further about the Antichrist or about the last coming of the Lord, but, imitating Ambrose, he comes down to opening up the sense of those words which concern the two in one bed and the two [women] grinding; and here, he says, the merit of the resurrection is shown, namely that the grace of rising again corresponds to the quality of one's living; and that there is so great a difference of resurrection in each individual that, of two sleeping alike and resting in one place, the taking up cannot be equal.
passages.notes: The allusion is to Luke 17:34–35 (cf. Matthew 24:40–41).

passages.original: Est enim aequus judex et justus; sed pro qualitate d horum rependat dileclionis affectum, et eum eligat, non qui verbis promptus, devotione piger,sed qui fuerit lingua tacitus, mente devotus, de quo dicit Propheta : Tacitum te faciens, sapiens videberis (Prov. XVII). De illo autem qui petulanter loquitur refert Scriptura : Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine, Domine, intrabit in regnum caelorum; sed qui fecerit volunta- tem meam (Matth.
passages.english: For he is a fair and just judge; but according to the quality of these he repays the disposition of love, and he chooses not the one who is ready with words but sluggish in devotion, but the one who is silent in tongue and devoted in mind, of whom the Prophet says: "By keeping yourself silent you will seem wise" (Prov. 17). But of the one who speaks impudently Scripture says: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does my will" (Matth.
passages.notes: The stray "d" before "horum" is taken as a footnote mark and omitted; "dileclionis" read as "dilectionis". The sentence and the reference break off at the end of the passage; the context shows it continues "VII)". "Rependat" and "eligat" are subjunctive in the Latin, perhaps following a preceding "Nunquid" or an implied purpose; they are rendered here as statements.
